title: Buoy 43, Off Cleyburn
passage:
At twenty past six the crane on the Marram takes the weight, and buoy 43 comes up out of the Cleyburn approaches trailing weed and a rope of grey mud. It lands on the afterdeck with a noise nobody bothers to talk over. The chain comes up after it, thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water, each link a hand's width across and slick. Ashore, a floating light is a small red shape printed on a chart. On deck it is a tonne of steel that has spent three years grinding a slow arc across the seabed.

That arc is the reason the tender exists. A floating aid is fixed to nothing; it is moored, and a mooring has to be slack. Chain longer than the depth lets the buoy lift to a sea instead of being pulled under by it, and the extra length soaks up the snatch that would otherwise be taken by the swivel above the sinker, the block of iron that holds the whole arrangement to the bottom. The trade calls the ratio of chain to depth the scope. What scope costs is a circle: wind and tide swing the buoy about its sinker, and the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over, so the light is somewhere inside that circle rather than on the cross printed on the chart. Wear is not spread evenly along the chain either. It gathers in the length that sweeps the ground and in the two or three links either side of the swivel, and a chain condemned for losing a fifth of its diameter is usually condemned on a single bad metre. The Marram's district holds two hundred and fourteen floating aids and lifts each of them once every three years. In flat water a lift, a scrape, a fresh lamp and a relay take about forty minutes.

Until 1968 the Gaunt Shoal was marked by a vessel rather than a buoy. The lightship moored there in 1911 with five men aboard, a lens, and a fog bell the older skippers still call the worst sound on that coast; she was withdrawn when the harbour board set the cost of her crew against a lamp on a hull that needed none. Her logs are kept at the office in Cleyburn and are mostly weather. They also carry, watch after watch, three bearings taken on the shore marks, because a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it. Osian Fewtrell, who served her last two winters, remembers the mate chalking a corrected position by the companionway. He remembers the painting more vividly: the whole hull, twice a year, at her mooring, in whatever swell there was. 'We knew the shoal was under us,' he says. 'Where we were over it was another question.'

How much scope to give is where the district's two authorities on the subject part company. Rufus Cadell has had the Marram for thirty-one years and lays his buoys long. A buoy that rides easy, he argues, comes through a February gale and a winter of ground swell; a buoy moored short takes the sea in its chain rather than in the water, and it is the chain that fails. 'You can put a light back exactly where the chart wants it,' he said on the second morning, 'and lose it in a gale the same month.' Naomi Prigent, a mooring engineer who has been fitting position loggers inside the hulls since 2019, does not dispute the gale. Her recordings put a figure on something the crews had only estimated: through the spring tides, the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together, and small craft now steer to a plotted mark on the assumption that they do not. Cadell has read the recordings and concedes the inshore aids, where the water is narrow. On the outer stations he has not moved.

Neither record disposes of the other. The district has lost two aids in ten years, both in the same storm, which is too thin a series to show whether a long mooring saves buoys or has merely been lucky; the wander is measured to the metre, and no grounding in the approaches has yet been traced to it. Prigent would like another ten years of loggers. Cadell would like a February. By nine o'clock buoy 43 has a scraped skirt, a new lamp and eleven fresh links at the swivel, and it goes back over the side on the scope its master chose. The chain runs out fast. Then the deck is hosed down.
– Fenella Moye

questions.prompt: What does the text say about the wear on a buoy's mooring chain?

options.text: Every link has lost about a fifth of its diameter by the end of a three-year cycle.
It builds up where the chain drags on the bottom and close to the swivel.
Salt corrosion accounts for more of it than any contact with the seabed does.
It is heaviest on the aids moored inshore, where the channel water is narrow.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 2, local passage order. WHY-KEY (B): the passage states that wear 'is not spread evenly along the chain either. It gathers in the length that sweeps the ground and in the two or three links either side of the swivel'. B recasts both halves of that sentence (ground contact plus the swivel neighbourhood) in different words, reusing no distinctive four-word run. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = quantifier_upgrade -- it keeps the real figure ('a chain condemned for losing a fifth of its diameter') but spreads it over 'every link' and pins it to the three-year lift, whereas the text says the opposite, that such a chain 'is usually condemned on a single bad metre'; tempting because both numbers are genuinely in the passage. C = outside_knowledge -- corrosion is a real and plausible cause of chain loss at sea, and the passage never mentions it; a reader supplying nautical common sense picks it. D = wrong_location / surface_word_match -- 'inshore aids, where the water is narrow' is lifted from the paragraph-4 concession about position, not about wear; the narrow water there bears on where a wandering light matters, not on how the chain is worn.

questions.prompt: What is implied about a buoy that is found some way from the position printed on the chart?

options.text: Its mooring chain must be about three times as long as the water is deep.
The less chain it has been given, the further from its charted cross it is likely to lie.
It may be riding the edge of the circle its chain allows, not dragging its sinker.
The district will lift it ahead of its turn in the three-year cycle.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 2. STEM-LAW: the stem describes only the observation (a light away from its charted cross) and does not entail what follows from it. WHY-KEY (C): the passage explains that 'wind and tide swing the buoy about its sinker, and the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over, so the light is somewhere inside that circle rather than on the cross printed on the chart.' The one-inch inference is that a wandering light is what a slack mooring is built to produce, and that the ground it can cover grows with the chain, so a buoy seen off the cross need not have shifted its sinker at all. C states exactly that, and no more: 'may be' offers the swing circle as the available reading, and does not claim a dragged sinker is impossible. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = too_literal / instance-as-rule -- it takes buoy 43's single measurement from paragraph 1 ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', a shade under three to one) and hardens one boat's arithmetic into a district-wide rule, which the passage refuses: how much scope to give is a judgement that varies, it is what the two authorities in paragraph 4 disagree about, Cadell 'lays his buoys long', and buoy 43 goes back over the side 'on the scope its master chose'. It is also retrieval offered where inference is asked: even a fixed ratio would say nothing about why this buoy is off its cross. B = reversed_causality -- it runs the passage's arrow backwards. The text ties the width of the wander to the length of the chain in the other direction ('the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over'), and paragraph 4 measures that same direction, since it is 'the buoys laid longest' that sit 'as much as 35 metres from their charted places'. On the passage's terms a short mooring buys a narrow circle and pays for it elsewhere -- 'a buoy moored short takes the sea in its chain rather than in the water, and it is the chain that fails' -- which is a chain that parts, not a light that wanders. B tempts because short mooring is the practice Cadell argues against, so a reader who has filed short chain under 'the bad option' expects it to be the thing that puts a light off its cross; its hedge ('is likely to lie') also keeps a measured form beside the measured key, so 'pick the qualified option' does not solve the item here either. D = too_far -- a two-step operational leap the text never takes; the passage describes a fixed three-year cycle and never mentions early lifts, so the reader has to import a maintenance policy of their own.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention the lightship that marked the Gaunt Shoal until 1968?

options.text: To show that a marked position was uncertain long before loggers went into the buoys.
To argue that the manned vessel held its station more faithfully than the buoy does.
To account for the disappearance of manned stations from the coast after the war.
To suggest that the old keepers may have watched their position more closely than today's crews.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-006 (purpose / function of a passage move), anchored in paragraph 3. WHY-KEY (A): the paragraph's load-bearing sentence is that the logs 'carry, watch after watch, three bearings taken on the shore marks, because a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it', closed by Fewtrell's two remarks, 'We knew the shoal was under us,' and 'Where we were over it was another question.' The function of the digression is therefore historical depth for the position problem the loggers now quantify -- the uncertainty is old, the instrument is new. A names that function without overstating it. WHY-DISTRACTORS: B = too_far / unsupported comparison -- the paragraph says the reverse if anything, that the lightship also wandered ('does not sit still either'); tempting to a reader who reads any mention of a retired manned station as nostalgia. C = wrong_location / outside_knowledge -- the passage gives one specific withdrawal reason for one vessel (crew cost set against 'a lamp on a hull that needed none') and never generalises to a coast-wide decline or to any post-war period; C sounds like the obvious historical frame and is not in the text. D = attribution / hedged decoy -- deliberately cautious in form ('may have') so that 'pick the hedged option' does not solve the item; it also answers the wrong question, since the paragraph is about the lightship's own position being uncertain, not about how attentive her keepers were beside anyone else. The passage never sets old keepers against present crews on a scale of care: the three bearings are there to show that a moored ship wandered too, and the modern figures come from Prigent's loggers, an engineer's instruments fitted since 2019, not from the tender crews' watchkeeping.

questions.prompt: What does the text say about Cadell's practice of laying his buoys long?

options.text: He has given it up since reading what Prigent's loggers recorded.
He defends it on the ground that long chain is cheaper to replace than a lost buoy.
He took it up after the storm in which the district lost two of its aids.
He has conceded the inshore aids to Prigent's figures but not the outer stations.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored at the end of paragraph 4, local passage order. WHY-KEY (D): 'Cadell has read the recordings and concedes the inshore aids, where the water is narrow. On the outer stations he has not moved.' D paraphrases that split position -- a partial retreat, not a defeat and not a refusal. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = polarity overshoot -- turns the partial concession into a full surrender; tempting because the sentence about reading the recordings does immediately precede a concession, and a skimmer stops there. B = outside_knowledge / substituted reason -- cost is a plausible mariner's argument and the passage does raise cost elsewhere (the lightship's crew set against a lamp), but Cadell's stated reason is mechanical: 'a buoy moored short takes the sea in its chain rather than in the water, and it is the chain that fails.' C = invented causality -- the two aids lost in one storm are real in the text, but they appear in the closing paragraph as a series too thin to settle the argument, not as the origin of Cadell's practice, which the passage attaches to no starting point at all.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: How the crew of a lightship held their station in the years before buoys marked the shoal.
What keeping a floating light on station involves, and an unsettled argument about slack.
Why position loggers ought to be fitted to every floating aid in the district.
The rising cost of maintaining navigation marks now that no station carries a crew.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text focus), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (B): the piece is built as a day's reportage on the tending craft -- the lift, the chain, the scope, the swing circle, the wear, the forty-minute turnaround -- with a disagreement about how much chain to give running through paragraphs 4 and 5 and left open ('Neither record disposes of the other'; 'Prigent would like another ten years of loggers. Cadell would like a February.'). B covers both the craft and the unresolved question of scope without claiming either side wins. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = scope_error / detail-as-main -- promotes the paragraph-3 digression to the whole text; it is one paragraph of five, and the lightship is used to date the problem, not to be the subject. C = surface_word_match -- borrows the loggers and turns them into a recommendation the writer never makes; the text reports what the loggers measured and explicitly leaves the practice unchanged on the outer stations. D = outside_knowledge / over-broad theme -- crew cost is mentioned once, as the reason one vessel was withdrawn in 1968, and nothing in the text tracks costs rising; it is the sort of theme a reader supplies when a passage mentions maintenance.
